Foreword

Status: PLANNED (the design is locked here first; §5's verbs ship together with this spec in the same change).

1. The property nobody has

A signature over a registry proves that whoever holds the key wrote those bytes. It says nothing about what was there last month. Yanking a row and re-signing is indistinguishable from the row never existing, and that is the one attack a mirror cannot detect: every mirror is happy to serve the smaller file.

Completeness is the missing property, and it needs machinery rather than good intentions:

  • append-only: the registry's history is a log that only grows;

  • provable: one row's presence is provable without shipping the log;

  • auditable: a row that disappeared without saying so is a NAMED alarm, not a diff somebody has to notice.

The machinery is an RFC 6962-shaped Merkle log (Certificate Transparency's shape) because it is the one construction third-party tooling already implements: inclusion proofs of log2(n) hashes, and a chain of heads that proves the log only grew.

2. The canonical snapshot

tebako registry snapshot <alias|path> renders every row of a registry document as ONE canonical line. Determinism is the premise — a snapshot that shifts when nothing changed is worthless as evidence:

Table 1
fieldrule
kindthe document's kind: value, verbatim
name@versionverbatim from the document (one line per row, so a version entry with N platform legs is N lines)
platformthe triplet, or universal; a variant arm renders <variant-id>:<universal|triplet> — the arm id never stands alone, so a universal arm can never be mistaken for a triplet
sha256the row's anchor digest, lowercase hex; - when the row declares none (a runtime index row)
stateactive, or withdrawn — spec 04's status: value verbatim, never a second spelling (§6)
keyidthe row's declared signer keyid when present, else -

Order: (kind, name, version, platform) — byte order, never document order. No timestamps, host names, comments or map iteration order enter a line: an author may reorder the YAML, rewrite its comments, or re-indent it, and the snapshot does not move. Two authors producing the same set of rows produce the same snapshot.

2.1 Where each column comes from (SSOT, never a re-derivation)

  • platform — a variants: arm renders its id from tebako_resolve::registry::variant_id() (spec 28 §2's one derivation). A second implementation of that derivation would produce snapshots that disagree with resolution, which is the one thing a transparency log cannot survive.

  • sha256 — the platform row's own sha256. A platforms: universal row carries NO digest column in the registry model (ReleaseRef holds a reference, not a hash; the anchor is the release's SHA256SUMS plus its attestation). Such a row renders -, and that is the honest value: this log proves the ROW SET is complete, while the release's own sums and attestations prove the BYTES. A ?sha256= pin inside the ref, when present, is rendered as that pin.

  • state — spec 04's status: verbatim (withdrawn when yanked), active when absent. Never a second vocabulary (§6).

  • keyid — the row's declared signer (signature.keyid) when present, else -.

--json emits the registry_log_schema: 1 document:

3. The tree

Leaves and nodes are domain-separated, so a leaf hash can never be mistaken for an interior node:

The fold is RFC 6962's: the largest power of two strictly smaller than the leaf count splits the tree, recursively. An odd tail is carried up, never padded — padding is what breaks third-party verifiers.

Inclusion proof for leaf i of n: the sibling hashes bottom-up, serialized as a JSON array of lowercase hex, plus the leaf's index and the tree's leaf count. A verifier recomputes the root from the line and the proof; nothing else is needed.

4. The log head and the chain law

Each snapshot is appended to the registry's log as one head record:

  • seq — 0, 1, 2, … ; strictly increasing, no gaps (a gap is a named error: the log was edited).

  • prev — the previous head's root (- for seq 0). A head whose prev does not match the previous head's root is a fork, named as such: the log diverged and nothing after that point can be trusted.

  • rows — the snapshot's leaf count; monotonic non-decreasing unless tombstones account for the difference (§6).

  • sig — detached OpenPGP over

    signed by the registry's declared head key (spec 09 §9.1's signing: block — the key the registry already carries; no new key class). The signature is verified against the pinned trust store, and an unknown signer is unknown-key (reported, never upgraded to trusted).

The log file is a head record per line, in seq order:

5. The verbs

  • snapshot renders §2's lines and root. --out writes them beside the registry for publication; without it they go to stdout (--json emits the document).

  • log verify checks, in order: every head's signature; the seq continuity; the prev chain (a fork is named at the head where it happens); and — when --registry is given — whether the document IS the row set the newest head sealed, by RECOMPUTING THE ROOT from the document's canonical rows. One number answers both halves: if the roots agree, no row could have been added, removed or edited without moving it. A rows decrease is reported separately (the chain alone cannot see tombstones), and a forced deletion therefore surfaces by name.

  • log prove emits the inclusion proof for --row against the newest head, and one proof per matching row: a version is often several rows (one per platform), and hiding all but one would understate what the registry says. It needs --registry as well as --row, because the canonical line cannot be reconstructed from a name alone — the line IS what is proved. --verify-root <hex> checks the proof against a root the caller obtained out of band: a user holding ONE 32-byte value can prove a row's membership without trusting the download that carried it.

Output discipline follows the toolchain's rule: --json documents on stdout alone (banner to stderr), human lines on stdout otherwise, exit codes per §7.

6. The tombstone law

A row may leave a registry; it may not leave silently. The vocabulary for leaving already exists and this spec does not invent a second one: spec 04's status: withdrawn (roadmap 85) is the tombstone — the resolver refuses a withdrawn row by name (WithdrawnPayload), listing surfaces render it as withdrawn, and release assets stay immutable.

Under the completeness law the ROW STAYS: tebako registry retire sets status: withdrawn on the version instead of deleting it, so the next snapshot renders the row as withdrawn and keeps it in the tree forever. A registry whose rows only ever disappear is a registry nobody can audit.

Withdrawal is the only legal way for a name to vanish from a snapshot or for rows to fall. --force still removes a row outright — an operator may need it — but the next log verify reports the disappearance by row name, and a forced removal is precisely the alarm the log exists to raise: never quiet.

7. Named errors and exit codes

Table 2
codeclassmeaning
71EX_TEBAKO_SIGNATUREa head's signature does not validate
72EX_TEBAKO_TRUSTa head's signer key is not in the trust store (unknown-key in JSON; the chain is still reported)
80EX_TEBAKO_LEDGERan integrity finding: a seq gap, a fork, a prev mismatch, a proof that does not verify, a row missing without a tombstone, or a tree/file inconsistency (spec 40 §6's ledger class — both streams are record streams whose integrity findings are one kind of event)
74EX_TEBAKO_IOa log or registry cannot be read or written
64EX_USAGEunknown flag, unparseable row reference, --verify-proof without a proof source

Every message names the row, the head, or the file — never "invalid input".

8. What this spec does not own

  • Registry document grammar and the signing: block: spec 04 and spec 37.

  • The signature mechanism and the trust store: spec 09.

  • Publication cadence and hosting: spec 13 and spec 37. This spec says what a published log must satisfy, never when to publish one.

  • Rotation of the head key: spec 09 §11's successor statement — a log signed under a successor key chains through prev like any other head.
